paras: The attempted lynching of Horn was a failed effort by unnamed men to lynch Horn, a man accused of rape, in Le Sueur County, Minnesota, shortly before his trial in late May 1882. The attempt collapsed when one of the lynching parties failed to arrive, and Horn was tried and sentenced to life imprisonment at Stillwater within days. The only report found treated the episode as a footnote to the court's speed.
The New Ulm Weekly Review called Horn "the ravisher" but gave no first name, no race, and no account of the alleged crime or its victim.

Before the Le Sueur county court met, according to the Weekly Review, "an incipient attempt was made to lynch Horn." It failed "on account of one of the lynching parties not coming to time." The paper did not say where or when the attempt took place, who took part, or where Horn was held.

Horn was indicted on a Wednesday and put on trial the next morning. That afternoon Judge McDonald sentenced him to what the paper called "a life-sojourn at Stillwater." No report of arrests or any inquiry into the would-be lynchers appears in the coverage.

The New Ulm Weekly Review carried the story in a four-sentence item on 31 May 1882, the only report found. Its emphasis fell on the court, which it said had disposed of Horn "in a prompt and expeditious manner." The lynching attempt appeared only in a closing sentence, which explained its failure as a matter of one party "not coming to time" and offered no comment. The item did not mention race.
